pull.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pull.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

Concept ACK.

Following on from what we discussed in person: a feature-ready, usable assumeUTXO is with P2P utxo snapshot sharing, no background validation, and potentially on by default. I don't think it's a state we want to be in.
That variant of assumeUTXO trusts the whole money supply and UTXO set without ever reconstructing it. Making that the default new user experience, for the dominant full node implementation, is a shift in what running a node means, I'd rather we lean on fewer assumptions, e.g. even removing assumevalid as default.

If the feature-ready version lands and most new nodes come up from a snapshot and never pull the history, then over time the archival nodes thin out and validating/having the chain's history becomes something only a handful of nodes still do. Worst case, you can recover your funds but not the history. Pruning already nudges us that way (though it's not on by default, and most users only prune when they actually need to), but a snapshot default would speed it up. It's a bit of an extreme scenario, but I don't think it's an implausible state to be in, if the direction is future ready assumeUTXO.

And as discussed, as-is it's not even that usable, loading the snapshot takes too long. I remember giving up when trying it for the first time. (This can be fixed though)

I've also hit a maintenance cost directly. e.g. in #34075 we do block building, and query the tip which needs the chainstate, and multiple chainstates make that harder than it should be. Any node component that needs chainstate has no guarantee the chainstate it grabbed is still live, and the active one can get swapped under it, so you end up holding onto the chainstate manager and re-fetching the active chainstate every time instead of just keeping a stable handle. The last seven commits here show what you get back once this is gone.

I do think there's probably still a group of users who'd want assumeUTXO like snapshot bootstrapping. But I'd rather that live outside the dominant full node, `libbitcoinkernel` c header api should gives downstream projects a way to embed a ready UTXO set without risking a consensus split? and with LLMs now, that node-like projects can easily be vibe coded.

Snapshot loading scales with the UTXO set size while IBD scales with chain length indeed, so there is some argument on the linear growth concern and that #35295 and your pruneassumevalid idea don't fully close that gap for a new node that validates/semi validates the chain history, and that gap only grows as the chain gets longer.
That's a genuine advantage of assumeUTXO. But I don't think it's worth the complexity and assumptions it adds to the the reference implementation.

@l0rinc should we do it through the usual deprecate then remove style? Also thanks for putting the demo together, having the removable code and the simplifications it shows is nice to see.

After the amount of time spent reviewing and testing assumeutxo, some folks might have a Stockholm syndroma removing assume utxo and me not the last...

More technically, it would has been possible to find an intermediary technical solution, where we would have kept the AssumeUTXO feature has an optional special build flag side-companion process available through a new `ipc/capnp/sidevalidation.cpp`. Somehow, the folks who wish to use AssumeUTXO would be able to do so, and this would ease diminish the maintenance burden for the libbitcoinkernel folks.

On a more usage level, I did share [few ideas](https://gnusha.org/pi/bitcoindev/CALZpt+FRPThy4qwYThXOY_YJWsGKJuCOqpX1Zt_8SqkeA4bQsg@mail.gmail.com/) in the past on how to use AssumeUTXO for second-layers reputation systems, see here. Never been practical, though it would have been interesting for second-layers nodes, as they would have been able to join the system "on-the-fly" by leveraging assumeutxo activate chainstate.

> This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

This is fine and useful.

But to be clear, I'm concept NACK on actually removing AssumeUTXO.

I think we should drop background validation first, as I suggested in #36557. After that we can reconsider if code complexity is still too high.

@ismaelsadeeq wrote:

> That variant of assumeUTXO trusts the whole money supply and UTXO set without ever reconstructing it. Making that the default new user experience, for the dominant full node implementation, is a shift in what running a node means, I'd rather we lean on fewer assumptions, e.g. even removing assumevalid as default.

(nit: the total supply can easily be checked against the issuance schedule. The distribution of the supply can't be checked.)

I don't think we should revisit `-assumevalid` in a discussion of removing AssumeUTXO, but it does raise an important point: we already allow users to skip part of validation and we even do it by default. And indeed perhaps we shouldn't, if the goal is to have every user verify everything even if they don't care and don't want to.

> If the feature-ready version lands and most new nodes come up from a snapshot and never pull the history, then over time the archival nodes thin out and validating/having the chain's history becomes something only a handful of nodes still do. 

Between the current reality of hardly anyone using AssumeUTXO, and the scenario you're describing, I think many decades will pass. By 2050 the blockchain might be 4 TB. The worst case UTXO set growth by then is 3+ TB, but at the current trend it might only be 35 GB. 

100x less stuff to download (and process) creates a strong incentive for new users to use a client that _does_ offer AssumeUTXO. It's a similar dynamic as with RBF: there's a limit to how far we can push against individual incentives to achieve network health. That goes for miner and for (non-miner) user incentives.

Also note that a user who didn't fully validate from genesis is still useful to the network if they provide mempool and (compact) block relay.

The big unpredictable factor here is Moore's law. In the optimistic scenario you'll download 4 TB in a few minutes in even the poorest and remote places on Earth. In a worst case scenario of technological regression, with a few quantum computers still surviving so we can't use compact signatures, everyone will just be using SPV or custodial wallets, because even after IBD keeping up with the chain would be too much.

@l0rinc wrote:

> Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.

I'm fine with refactoring things towards a cleaner approach, but it's not realistic to expect that if we remove this, it's going to come back. I'm also not convinced that the feature is so problematic that it needs to be temporarily removed. Even UPnP wasn't removed, merely disabled by default after the RCE vulnerabilities, but AssumeUTXO is already opt-in (and should stay that way).

concept ACK

Similar to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36598#issuecomment-6338865042 , I've been mulling on the future of this feature. 

I think the grand vision for the feature is too limited to actually be of general use. The current  feature is incomplete, and not particularly fast, and is not a bandwidth saver either.

The purpose of the feature was to capture marginal users that would not have run a node, but now will, at a subtly different trust model. My prior is to doubt this, and all subsequent evidence has been one sided sadly. Node-in-a-box, as far as we know, continued what they've always done,

Grand future aside, the code has also been a long source of bugs, of varying severity. I can't speak to who's "fault" this is, but given the current architecture, it's a simple reality. This is ongoing maintenance cost which means it shouldn't simply be ignored. We should complete the project, or cut our losses and harden the codebase we have left.
